newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters settle 15-day delivery strike.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters settle 15-day delivery strike.

text.p: Teamster leaders prepared Tuesday to vote on the contract with United Parcel Service as UPS said it would try to win back $650 million in business lost during the nation's biggest strike in two decades.

At picket lines near UPS headquarters in Atlanta, thousands of Teamster union members cheered the tentative pact announced late Monday to settle the 15-day-old strike, which was widely seen as a victory for organized labor.

President Bill Clinton called the settlement "a good thing for the country. It's good for the company, good for the employees," he said, speaking to reporters while on vacation on Martha's Vineyard, off the Massachusetts coast.
"It's a victory for the proposition that you can treat your employees well and make money. That's what I wanted to prove from the time I became president," he said.

UPS Chairman James Kelly said the company's fleet of brown vans would be running full-out by Wednesday, while officials at the world's largest package delivery company would contact customers to try to win back business lost during the strike.

Teamsters President Ron Carey said the 185,000 striking workers, who received $55 a week in union strike benefits, could go back to work Wednesday. Local union leaders will meet in Washington later Tuesday to vote on the deal, which is subject to approval by Teamster members.

The breakthrough came Monday night after almost 90 hours of negotiations at a Washington hotel. A federal mediator guided the talks and Labor Secretary Alexis Herman was in the hotel and kept pushing the two sides to keep talking.

Carey said the union had won sweeping concessions from UPS, which normally uses its own fleet of planes and the familiar brown vans to deliver 12 million packages a day, dominating the shipping business in the United States. Its annual sales are $22.4 billion.
Under the agreement, UPS will convert 10,000 part-time jobs into full-time jobs over five years and hourly wage rates will rise as much as 36 percent, Carey told a news conference.

The bad news for the union was that UPS said it may cut jobs because of business lost during the strike. The U.S. Postal Service and Federal Express Corp., among others, saw a surge in demand for shipments after the strike began Aug. 4.
"Unfortunately, 5 percent of our business is susceptible to being lost. ... We're predicting 15,000 (jobs) will not be necessary," UPS spokesman Ken Sternad told Cable News Network.
"We're hoping it (the job losses) will be less than that," Kelly said later at a news conference in Atlanta.
Carey, who had staked his reputation on the outcome of the strike, hailed the result as a turning point for a union movement that has lost much of its former power.

"This strike marks a new era. American workers have shown that we (can) stand up to corporate greed. This victory shows that American workers are on the move again. This is the direction corporate America ought to be taking," he said.

Striking sorters, loaders and drivers had won the battle for public opinion, with Americans supporting the workers and their objections to the growing use of part-time employees, polls showed. Teamster officials, with the support of the AFL-CIO labor federation, repeatedly made the point that part-time wages were not sufficient for most families.
Labor supporters said the dispute showed it was time to redress the balance between workers and large companies that have benefited from more than six years of economic growth.
Labor Secretary Herman declined to say who she thought had won the strike, but said the settlement could set a standard for other collective bargaining agreements.

"This agreement certainly has taken historic steps ... and I think it becomes a model for other companies today as we look at the question not only of good wages but also health benefits and retirement security for workers," she said.
In addition to part-timers, pensions were another key issue in the dispute. UPS management wanted to replace a Teamsters multi-employer plan with a company-controlled plan.
Carey said the union had its way on the pension fund and won generous new benefits. He said a retiring 30-year worker would get monthly benefits of $3,000 or more.

The pact also would phase out the use of subcontractors, except during holiday peak periods, giving the jobs instead to UPS workers. Full-time workers' wages would rise $3.10 to as much as $23 an hour under the five-year pact while part-time wages would increase $4.10 to about $15 an hour.
In addition, if UPS wants to raise the limits on package weight again, it must negotiate with the union, Carey said.

The union representing UPS pilots, who had refused to work during the Teamsters strike, welcomed the agreement and said it asked to meet with UPS officials to draw up a return-to-work plan once the Teamsters strike officially ends.
